title: An Invitation
author: Cammie Passey
summary: Cammie Passey, now National Director of Lower School Curriculum for Great Hearts, recounts a formative moment from her first year at a classical charter school fourteen years ago. An experienced public school teacher confident in her classroom management, she had adapted her longtime motto to read 'You Can Do Anything You Want as Long as it is Virtuous,' only to have her headmaster pause, read it aloud, and invite her to consider whether virtue is relative and what students should truly be pointed toward. He issued no directive, but the conversation left her humiliated, defensive, and unsure she belonged. Passey uses the episode to trace her understanding of classical education from its trappings, such as rigorous academics, great books, and comportment standards, to its end: the cultivation of intellectual and moral virtue and helping students answer 'Who am I and what am I to do with my life?' Her central move is to present the headmaster's invitation to dialogue as itself a model of classical education, which invites students across every discipline to encounter reality. She closes by reassuring teachers without philosophy backgrounds that they belong if they accept that invitation.
points: Passey's headmaster corrected her classroom motto not by directive but by asking whether virtue is up for individual interpretation, modeling leadership through questions.
She came to see her revised motto as still a behavior-management gimmick, recognizing that drawing students toward virtue does not depend on slogans.
Early on she defined classical education by its trappings, but now sees curriculum, books, and standards as serving the cultivation of intellectual and moral virtue.
The purpose she names is not merely creating lifelong learners but forming souls by helping students ask who they are and what to do with their lives.
Every discipline, from verb conjugation to athletics, is presented as an invitation for students to encounter real truths about existence.
quotes: You can do anything you want as long as it is virtuous,” he read aloud, clearly searching for the right way to kindly engage me in a corrective conversation about my classroom décor. We were, after all, preparing for the upcoming meet-the-teacher night.

He listened graciously, then asked me to consider what we should truly be pointing our students toward. He asked me to reflect on the nature of goodness and whether virtue is relative; if it’s up for individual interpretation. He didn’t shame me; he didn’t give me the directive to change what I had displayed; he simply invited me to have a conversation.

I was humiliated and even a little angry. My entire management structure had been questioned, and my classroom was always well-managed. Not for the last time, I felt out of place and small and wondered if classical education was a good fit. If I was a good fit.

In retrospect, I see that even the revamped motto was still gimmicky; after 14 years in a classical network, I know there are better ways to establish appropriate learning conditions and draw students’ attention to virtue. I know that I don’t need to rely on gimmicks, mottos, or slogans. The invitation my headmaster extended to me that afternoon to consider something deeper left an impression.

The aim of a classical education is to habituate students toward the pursuit of excellence, and our work as its practitioners is to help the students answer the questions, “Who am I and what am I to do with my life?” Our call is not merely to create lifelong learners; it is to form souls.

I felt out of my depth, and my visceral response to the discomfort of being challenged, of being a novice, was defensiveness, bordering on contempt. But because I was invited into the conversation, because I was asked to actively participate in dialogue about reality, something in my soul expanded. And that, the invitation to behold reality, is what we have the privilege of offering every day as classical educators.
